title: Cap. VII: reprobation decree not thrust into all acts — common love; Rom. 2:4-5
pass_a_gloss: Further, that deep and secret decree of non-election or reprobation is not so awkwardly to be thrust into all God's actions, as if with the non-elect God did nothing, except from this decree of non-election. For although God was unwilling to pity certain ones so far as to decree to lead them infallibly to eternal life, and willed to destine the same to ruin with their sin intervening, yet while they act on earth, and especially within the pale of the Church, in conferring both bodily and spiritual benefits, and such as by the nature of the thing tend to salvation, he does many things with them from common love or φιλανθρωπία, with which he pursues the whole human race, many things from the covenant by which according to his ordination he bestows certain supernatural benefits on all members of the visible Church. In the event all these gifts of God become noxious and pernicious to the reprobate: yet it is not to be said or felt that God on account of the decree of reprobation intends the abuse of his gifts, and with hostile mind supplies them to the non-elect, that abusing these he may punish and destroy them. Rather Paul's sentence is to be embraced, who shows that God does many things with the non-elect from that overflowing benignity which diffuses itself to all men, though not in equal degree or measure. Hither look those things, Rom. 2:4-5: Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and patience, not knowing that thou art led by the benignity of God unto repentance? But according to thy hardness, and heart that knows not to repent, thou treasurest up wrath for thyself, etc.
pass_b_english: Further: that deep secret decree of non-election or reprobation must not be awkwardly stuffed into every act of God, as if with the non-elect he did nothing except from that decree. Though he would not pity some so far as to decree their infallible leading to eternal life, and willed to destine them to ruin with their sin intervening, yet while they live on earth — especially within the Church's pale — in giving bodily and spiritual benefits that by nature tend to salvation, he does much with them from common love or φιλανθρωπία toward the whole human race, and much from the covenant by which he lavishes certain supernatural benefits on all members of the visible Church. In the event those gifts become noxious to the reprobate — yet one must not say God by the reprobation decree intends abuse of his gifts, and hostilely supplies them to the non-elect so that abusing them they may be punished and destroyed. Rather take Paul's word: God does much with the non-elect from that overflowing kindness that spreads to all, though not in equal measure (Rom. 2:4-5 — or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience, not knowing God's kindness leads you to repentance? But by your hardness you treasure up wrath).
source_text: Porro, altum illud et arcanum non-electionis sive reprobationis decretum non est ita omnibus Dei actionibus importune ingerendum, quasi cum non-electis Deus nihil ageret, nisi ex hoc non-electionis decreto. Utcunque enim Deus quorundam noluerit eousque misereri, ut decernet eos ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter perducere, atque voluerit cosdem interveniente illorum peccato exitio destinare, tamen dum agunt in terris, atque praesertim intra Ecclesiae septa, in conferendis tum beneficiis corporalibus tum spiritualibus, atque ad salutem ex rei natura tendentibus, multa cum illis agit ex amore communi sive φιλανθρωπίᾳ, qua universum genus humanum prosequitur, multa ex foedere, quo secundum suam ordinationem omnibus Ecclesiae visibilis membris supernaturalia quaedam beneficia largitur. In eventu haec omnia Dei dona fiunt reprobis noxia et perniciosa: non tamen dicendum aut sentiendum est, Deum propter decretum reprobationis intendere abusum donorum suorum, et hostili animo ea suppeditare non-electis, ut eos hisce abutentes puniat ac perdat. Pauli potius sententia amplectanda est, qui ostendit Deum cum non-electis multa agere ex illa redundanti benignitate quae ad omnes homines se diffundit, quamvis non pari gradu aut mensura. Huc spectant illa, Rom. ii. 4. 5: An divitias bonitatis ejus et patientiae contemnis, ignorans te benignitate Dei ad resipiscentiam deduci? Sed pro duritia tua, et corde quod resipiscere nescit, thesaurizas tibi iram, etc.
